newsitem.title: VIETNAM: FEATURE - U.S. surgeons build bridges in Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - U.S. surgeons build bridges in Vietnam.

text.p: Au Thi Suu, 11, sits on an operating table, crying, in a provincial hospital two hours by road to the north of Hanoi, Vietnam's capital.

After a long journey with her father by foot and local bus, followed by days of nervous waiting in the district capital, she is about to go under the knife of a surgeon from New York in an operation aimed at changing her appearance, and her life.

The provincial hospital surgery in Thai Nguyen offers little comfort. The bare room with its grim, white-tile walls is redolent of an era of more frightening surgical intervention. A single light is positioned over the patient.
Moments later the process begins.
Suu suffers a cleft lip and palate -- a physical, and often psychologically scarring, disfiguration that has all but disappeared in the West thanks to routine surgical intervention.
But in Vietnam, where per capita income is little above $200 per year and where medical facilities and know-how are spread thin, many victims suffer their fate without hope of change.

The small team of U.S. nurses and doctors operating on Suu are members of Operation Smile, an organisation that sends volunteer U.S. reconstructive surgery teams on goodwill visits around the world to repair such deformities.
On its current visit to Vietnam, the team has been operating on children and young adults here and in Can Tho in the country's southern Mekong Delta.
In many senses it's a classic American goodwill mission, involving volunteer medical staff, expertise, enthusiasm, children and tangible results.
But for any U.S. mission to Vietnam, things are rarely that simple.
On a previous trip, four team members were arrested, for reasons which were not clear.
People connected with the current visit say the team has also experienced what they describe as "misunderstandings" with local officials and police over matters of money and security.

"Our hotel was swarming with police," said one team member who asked not to be named. "We've got Vietnamese-Americans among us for whom this is the first time they've been back here. Obviously some of them get pretty scared."

Despite the problems, the work goes on. Occasional heated difficulties are seen as fleeting obstacles in a broader mission to help heal the lingering and far deeper wound in post-war relations between Vietnam and the United States.
Since the late 1980s, Operation Smile has been a part of U.S. efforts to build bridges and trust with its former foe.
General John Vessey, former Chairman of the U.S. Joint Chiefs of Staff, asked a small team of medical volunteers to visit Vietnam in 1988 to operate on around 100 children who suffered birth defects.

The move helped towards the release of remains of missing American servicemen from the Vietnam War. The group's first formal mission in Vietnam began in 1989, six years before the two countries ended formal animosity and normalised relations.

Back at the Thai Nguyen hospital, Suu, still unconscious, is carried to a recovery room. Her father, Au Van Va -- a member of one of Vietnam's 54 ethnic minorities -- peers anxiously through a window from the courtyard outside.
Within minutes, he is admitted. As Suu comes around his expression turns from relief to joy.
"Very good. I'm very happy. She's now become beautiful...very good," he says, finding himself short on words.
Team member Valerie Barrett, on her first trip to Vietnam, echoes the sentiment and laughs when asked why she got involved.
"Even though we can't really communicate unless we have a translator...you don't need to be able to speak the language. The mothers have been very tearful and smiling and very happy," she says.
